This relatively small size at parturition suggests that the yolk-dependent embryonic phase yields a well-developed but still vulnerable pup, which must immediately begin foraging on small benthic invertebrates in the deep-sea environment. The species exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in the timing of reproductive maturation, a pattern commonly observed among chimaeriform fishes. Under the cold thermal regime typical of its habitat, approximately 7.1 °C [T = 7.1 °C], males attain sexual maturity after about 16 years since birth [tp = about 16 years since birth], whereas females require a substantially longer developmental period, reaching puberty at approximately 21 years since birth [tp = approximately 21 years since birth]. This extended juvenile phase in females is likely linked to the energetic demands of producing large, lipid-rich yolked eggs.

At the stable temperature of 7.1 °C [T = 7.1 °C], females reach puberty upon attaining a total length of 84.8 centimeters [Lp = 84.8 centimeters], a measurement that underscores their need for a larger body cavity to accommodate developing oocytes. Males, in contrast, become reproductively mature at a notably smaller total length, measuring 68.8 centimeters [Lp = 68.8 centimeters]. This disparity in size at maturity is consistent with a mating system where males likely compete for access to females, but the energetic investment in gamete production is substantially lower than the ovarian investment required by females. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is 165 centimeters [Li = 165 centimeters], a maximum size that appears to represent the upper boundary of somatic growth before physiological senescence begins to constrain further increases in body dimensions.

Reproductive output in Rhinochimaera pacifica is remarkably low, consistent with a K-selected life history adapted to the stable but resource-poor deep-sea environment. The maximum reproductive rate for this species, observed under the prevailing water temperature of 7.1 °C [T = 7.1 °C], is estimated from the presence of enlarged ovarian oocytes in females measuring 80 centimeters total length. This observation suggests that only a single reproductive event occurs every 36.5 days on average, yielding approximately 10 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 10 offspring per year]. Such a low fecundity implies that each pup benefits from considerable maternal investment, likely in the form of a large, nutrient-rich yolk that supports an extended embryonic development within the protective egg capsule. The modest reproductive output is further constrained by the slow metabolic rates typical of cold-water chondrichthyans.

The maximum recorded wet weight for an adult Pacific spookfish reaches an impressive 22,500 grams [Wwi = 22,500 grams], a body mass consistent with the allometric scaling relationship derived from its ultimate length. This large size is achieved over an exceptionally long lifespan; individuals are estimated to live for approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] when residing in waters at 7.1 °C [T = 7.1 °C]. This remarkable longevity, coupled with delayed maturity and low fecundity, renders the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as population turnover is exceedingly slow. The deep, cold waters of the continental slope, where temperatures hover around 7.1 °C, provide a stable thermal environment that minimizes metabolic costs but also limits the scope for rapid growth and early reproduction.

Comparative analyses with other chimaeroid fishes reveal that Rhinochimaera pacifica occupies a life-history continuum somewhere between the relatively short-lived, early-maturing callorhinchids and the extremely long-lived, late-maturing genera such as Harriotta. The extended time since birth at puberty for both sexes, measured at 16 years for males and 21 years for females under the ambient temperature of 7.1 °C [T = 7.1 °C], places this species among the slowest-maturing cartilaginous fishes known. In terms of body composition, the substantial ultimate wet weight of 22.5 kilograms [Wwi = 22.5 kilograms], derived from its maximum recorded length of 165 centimeters [Li = 165 centimeters], reflects a robust, muscular body adapted for sustained swimming in the deep water column. The overall life-history strategy, characterized by extreme longevity, late maturity, and minimal reproductive output, underscores the need for careful management of any potential fishery targeting this deep-sea species.
